content.title: I have many concerns on this submission. -- After reading the rebuttal, nothing new in this paper. The authors turn a deaf ear on the literature. The robustness is due to obfuscated gradient.
content.review:
This paper proposes to do adversarial defense by adding noise to Resnets and model ensemble, which seems not new to me. I have substantial concerns from the model to experiments about this paper.


Major comments:

1. My first major concern is what is the difference between this paper compared and the paper ``````"Resnets ensemble via the Feynman-Kac formalism to improve natural and robust accuracies, NeurIPS, 2019’’. In this paper, the authors have already interpreted the adversarial vulnerability of ResNets from a transport equation viewpoint and proposed to ensemble the noise injected ResNets informed by the Feynman-Kac formula. The work in NeurIPS 2019 has been restated in the section ``Robustness of stochastic Ito resnets ensemble’’. Please justify this. Furthermore, the authors ignored all the existing works along the direction of injecting noise into neural networks to improve robustness, which are the most related works to this paper. Just name a few here. "Towards robust neural networks via random self-ensemble, ECCV, 2018". "Resnets ensemble via the Feynman-Kac formalism to improve natural and robust accuracies, NeurIPS, 2019". "Parametric noise injection: Trainable randomness to improve deep neural network robustness against adversarial attack, CVPR, 2019". 

2. I am concerned about modeling Resnets as an ODE, why is the scale of different layers consistent; in particular, how can you consider the step size goes to zero? In ResNets, the dimension of different layers varies, how is this reflected in the ODE model? The derivation in section 3 is very questionable. The authors need to justify why making an ODE model of Resnet makes sense. 

3. How is the backpropagation of noise injected ResNet done?

4. The experiment parts did not consider the obfuscated gradient at all! This makes me feel the reported robustness results are not trustworthy. Let me elaborate here: 1) Due to noise injection, the gradient used in the attack is not the true gradient, which makes an obfuscated gradient. To attack the model, the author should use the EoT attack. 2) The authors should attack models with IFGSM with more iterations, say 1000 iterations, and compare with PGD adversarial training in the same setting. 3) The ensemble of models increases the model capacity, which makes comparison unfair. As is pointed out in ``"Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks, ICLR 2018’’, model capacity is crucial for adversarial robustness. 4) The authors may also attack their model with gradient-free attacks. 

5. In a nutshell, to my understanding, the algorithm proposed in this paper has been published before and the reported robustness is based on obfuscated gradient, which is well known in this community. Based on these, I have to give a very low score for this submission.


Minor comments:

1. Second paragraph: the authors state that preprocessing methods can improve robustness. This is questionable, as pointed in the paper "``Obfuscated gradients give a false sense of security: circumventing defenses to adversarial examples, ICML 2018’’, these approaches did not really improve robustness.

2. Second paragraph: the authors state that these theoretical guarantees on worst-case inputs hold only for small perturbation. This seems wrong, please read the certification papers carefully and check the certified robust radius. For instance, ``"Certified adversarial robustness via randomized smoothing, ICML 2019’’. I did not see a noticeable advantage of the robustness of this paper over existing certifications.

3. Typos still exist. Please check the paper carefully.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
* Comparison with Related Work (````NeurIPS 2019, CVPR 2019)

We thank the reviewer for pointing us to this related work. Our work differs from these in some important aspects: 

- The NeurIPS 2019 paper uses adversarial training in conjunction with stochastic ResNets. On the other hand, our approach does not use any adversarial training at all. This makes our approach faster and generalizable to unseen attacks. Hence, our approach is truly based on the stochastic dynamical model of DNNs. 
We currently compared our approach with the best performance reported in the NeurIPS 2019 paper for ResNets (Table 1 of the NeurIPS paper, last row, col 4) is 61.82, and our approach achieves an accuracy of 88.24% (table 4, row 2, col 3) for the same FGSM attack (norm and attack strength). We will add a more detailed experimental comparison with NeurIPS 2019. 

- The CVPR 2019 paper also learns the injected noise from training using adversarial examples. We use noise during training but do not learn it and hence, do not require exposure to adversarial examples. This is crucial to being able to generalize to new kinds of adversarial attacks. Our approach ensures that the learned model is inherently robust. 

* Modeling Resnets as an ODE

The ODE modeling of ResNet with different layers is standard and has been recently revived in papers such as Chen, R.T., Rubanova, Y., Bettencourt, J. and Duvenaud, D.K., Neural ordinary differential equations. In Advances in neural information processing systems 2018, as well as the NeurIPS19 cited by the reviewer. We utilize this formalism. Our innovation is in the addition of noise during training to make our model robust. 
At the end of Section 3, Page 4, we emphasize that the noise injected is of different scales for different layers. The injection of noise is through sampling which allows us to train our models using standard backpropagation.  


* Obfuscated Gradient 

We do not just inject noise during inference which would have been an approach using the obfuscation of gradient. We train our models after injecting noise which makes them robust to perturbations and hence, resilient to adversarial attacks. In our experiments, we have found that removing the noise during the inference step does not cause a significant change in the robustness of the trained neural networks, and hence, the source of our robustness is not the obfuscation of gradients. We have compared with another ensemble approach [Tianyu Pang, Kun Xu, Chao Du, Ning Chen, and Jun Zhu. Improving adversarial robustness via promoting ensemble diversity. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 2019.] in Table 1, Row 5 of our paper.  Our approach achieves an accuracy of 84.6% as compared to 48.4% in the previous ensemble approach. 

* Preprocessing Methods 

This was mentioned in the review of related work while discussing techniques that depend on preprocessing. We also note in that discussion that preprocessing “makes these approaches susceptible to newer attack strategies”.  Our approach does not depend on preprocessing. 


* Theoretical Guarantees on Worst-case Inputs

This discussion is also in the context of describing the related work. The “worst-case inputs” are from the formal verification literature  (Dutta et al., 2018). The statistical approaches to certifiable defense scale much better but do not provide the absolute worst-case input perturbations ; our statement about “worst-case” is referring to these perturbations.

content.title: This work is very incremental and the authors do not understand obfuscated gradient at all
content.comment:
The authors clarified that the difference between this work and the NeurIPS 2019 work is only the authors used natural training to get fake robustness, while NeurIPS 2019 paper used adversarial training.

Let me explain why your robustness is fake!

1. You have noise in your neural network, which makes your obtained gradient is not the adversarial direction. To eliminate this, the ICML 2018 paper proposed the expectation over the random transformation attack, which will alleviate this obfuscation.

2. To further verify your defense is based on obfuscated gradient, you can perform black box attack. If a weaker attack can attack your model more effectively, then it is a red flag that your attack is based on obfuscate gradients. Here, I cite the original sentence from ICML 2018 paper " Identifying Obfuscated & Masked Gradients: Black-box attacks are better than white-box attacks. The black-box threat model is a strict subset of the white-box threat model, so attacks in the white-box setting should perform better; if a defense is obfuscating gradients, then black-box attacks (which do not use the gradient) often perform better than white-box attacks (Papernot et al., 2017)." 

3. The current attacks are all gradient based attack, while you do not have the right gradient to attack your model. To show the obfuscated gradient, you should also test on the gradient free attacks.



Based on the authors' response, I am almost sure that the current work is almost nothing new and the robustness is fake. So I decided to futher reduce my rating on this paper.

content.title: Connection with obfuscation
content.comment: We respectfully disagree. As summarized in our response, switching the noise completely off during inference also attains high robustness which clearly demonstrates that the resilience is not because of the "obfuscated gradient". Instead, the robustness arises due to the training process (with noise) making the model less susceptible to the adversarial perturbations. The reviewer is misunderstanding the basic contribution of the paper.

content.comment:
Please provide black-box attack and gradient-free attack results. 


Do you understand the public comments?

##############
I'd like to better understand the results.

First, what are the parameters of PGD used to run the attack? How many iterations of gradient descent, random restart trials, are used?

Second, does the attack take into account the fact that the defense is a stochastic ensemble? Prior defenses that have been stochastic (e.g., SAP ICLR'18, k-WTA ICLR'20) have been broken because the attacks haven't properly averaged over randomness.

Third, I'd like to check my understanding of the results. This paper claims for CIFAR-10 a 74% robust accuracy (with abstaining) at l_inf eps=32/255. No other paper has achieved stronger than ~60% at eps=8/255. To clarify: is this paper is claiming that under a 4x larger distortion bound it can improve on prior work by 10 percentage points?

#############


Before you provide these justifications, I have to rate your work at "Trivial or wrong", since I fear you do not understand obfuscated gradient at all and claimed the wrong robustness. If you can justify your answer with more evidence, I am happy to raise my rating.

content.title: Exp Details
content.comment:
As we mentioned, removing stochastic aspect during inference still maintains robustness. So, the concern of stochasticity during inference being the sole source of robustness is unfounded. It is the training process which imparts resilience.

Each table shows the type of attack and the relevant parameters. We use 20 iterations for reported numbers and kept it the same for comparison with other techniques.

Table 1 in our paper identifies the leap in the robustness (also reported in a public comment) from SOTA and was the main motivation for writing this paper. Our approach uses a novel technique to train robust network ensembles as Ito processes which has not been studied in literature before So, it is not surprising that our results are significantly better.

content.title: Several numerical approaches to identify obfuscated gradient
content.comment:
I do not want to argue with you on your experiments part anymore, which is fake robustness to any people who understand obfuscated gradient.

Let me give you a few suggestions on how to verify your robustness is not due to an obfuscated gradient.

1. Perform black-box attacks, and if the black-box attacks can attack your model more efficiently then the white-box attack. Then the robustness is due to the obfuscated gradient.

2. Perform gradient free attack, and if the strong gradient free attack can break your defense. Then your stochastic approach is due to obfuscated gradients.

3. Instead of using 20 iterations, you should use more iterations and compare them to the baseline adversarial training. It is known that the robust accuracy of adversarial training will not further drop much even you use IFGSM1000 or even more iteration. But if your robustness drops significantly, then the accuracy is because of obfuscated gradients again.

4. Apply EoT to compute the gradient.

If you can eliminate all the above three possibilities. Then please respond to Nicholas Carlini. If your model is truly robust, I am willing to give it the highest rating, since it seems a breakthrough in the robust machine learning community.

Before you provide these evidences, I do not want to discuss it with you anymore. I am responsible enough to your submission.

content.title: Let's keep the discussion civil
content.comment:
I just want to chime in on this thread because there's now some discussion around my public comment.

Saying that something should be obvious to people who have a "basic" knowledge of adversarial examples or dynamic systems is not helpful to either case. (The average ICLR reviewer won't be an expert in dynamic systems---I'm certainly not---and it may be helpful to provide a sufficiently clear justification that the average ML reader might understand. Similarly, the average author couldn't hope to read all 2000+ adversarial example papers---I certainly haven't.)

We all can probably agree that the claims of the paper are very strong. We can all also agree that whether or not there's some form of gradient making going on here, the important question to answer is if the network truly is robust, or if it an artifact of how the evaluation was performed.

Let me try to paraphrase my understanding of R2 and of the authors. R2 is questioning the correctness of the evaluation because the network is randomized, which is a common reason why defenses tend to have flaws in the evaluation. The authors respond that even when removing any inference-time randomness, the results still stand. Therefore inference time randomness can't (solely) be responsible for any gradient obfuscation. 

What I think R2 is trying to get at here, though, is that typically when a paper makes extraordinary claims, we should expect extraordinary evidence. If a paper were to claim 3% ImageNet top-1 error (the current SOTA is ~12% error) reviewers would be rightly skeptical. That is essentially what this paper is doing.

Importantly, when this paper compares to Pang et al. 2019, that defense is not completely broken and offers 0% accuracy (see Section 11 of Tramer et al. 2020 ("On adaptive attacks")). The fact that this paper bears similarity to that paper indicates it may be worth studying the robustness of the proposed approach more carefully.

Speaking only for myself, after trying to read this paper carefully, I don't feel that I have enough information to try and reproduce the implementation or the claims. There's a lot of theory in Section 3, but it is skipping over a lot of important details. Concretely what should one do (an algorithm would help) to train a model with the proposed approach? How are the multiple networks aggregated to form a single prediction? Section 4 similarly misses over some details on attack setup. I don't see any discussion of PGD hyperaparameters or how the attack was set up.

It may help, for example, to release code (+ pretrained models) to justify the robustness claims, as most prior work has done.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for identifying our contribution to be original and our paper to be well written. We address the concerns of the reviewer below.

*quality The paper present to the setting of stochastic ODE, which is a very interesting idea. The authors argues such neural nets are stable, but the argument is hand waving and lacks theory.

We have mathematically shown that the Lipschitz constant for ODE models of ResNets has a O(1/T) dependence on the depth T of the network while the Lipschitz constant for our stochastic model has a O(1/T^2) dependence on the depth of the network. This result theoretically explains the observed empirical robustness of our stochastic neural networks. We will add this result to the paper.

*significance Although the paper's idea is interesting, the idea seems very straightforward, and marginally incremental. If the authors can contribute more provable theoretical robustness guarantees, then the paper would be a good accept. 

The significant empirical improvement and the exploitation of the insight of stochastic dynamics is clearly novel and improves on existing work. Beyond the mathematical result mentioned above, our experiments compare very favorably to existing ensemble-based approach as demonstrated in Table 1. In section 4, we have shown the following on both CIFAR-10 and ImageNet data sets:
Q1: The Itoˆ ensemble achieves competitive accuracy on benign inputs.
Q2: The stochastic Ito ensemble is robust against diverse adversarial attacks with different attack strengths.
Q3: The robustness of the stochastic Ito ensemble improves with the size of the ensemble.
Q4: We studied how the diffusion term ω can be controlled to trade-off robustness and accuracy.

display_title: Ensembles of neural networks are more robust to perturbations of inputs

content.title: Ensembles of neural networks are more robust to perturbations of inputs
content.review:
The authors propose a strategy to make the original ResNet more robust through adding a Brownian motion term to the ODE corresponding to the original ResNet model and taking ensembles of different disctretizations of the resulting stochastic differential equation. Greatly improved robustness is demonstrated on standard tasks, with a small decrease in accuracy of performance. The technique is on appearance simple, straightforward to use and works well in practice.

One crucial difference that the authors point out which sets their work apart from previous work in this area is not having to make the model robust to a specially selected set of adversarial attacks, or to limit the size of the adversarial perturbation that a model is able to withstand.

Some comments. 

1. What about trying ensembles where the $\omega$ term can be different for different members of the ensemble? I would predict that such ensembles would be more beneficial than ones that use a single value of $\omega$. Like an ensemble with $\omega = 0.2$ for 10 members and $\omega = 0.4$ for 10 members.

2. Can these techniques for robustness be generalized beyond ResNets? Are there equivalent techniques for other models that the authors know of?

3. No details on the training or inference are provided, making reproduction of the results in this paper very challenging for the user. Could you please make it more clear how exactly the proposed networks are trained? As I can guess, each network in the ensemble uses a different discretization. This raises the question --- namely, how these different discretizations of SDEs computed and how the backpropagation procedure to find the weights of the network is done? You should mention what sort of packages can be used to accomplish this. Also, once each network in the ensemble is obtained, how exactly are "independent inferences" drawn from each model?

4. The use of ensembles of several models to provide robustness has been widely used in the machine learning literature before. The authors should review or at least mention other approaches to constructing ensembles and comment on why their method provides an advantage versus existing ones. What is it about adding a Brownian motion term to an SDE that acts to help with improving robustness?

Overall, however, the results seem pretty impressive to me and the technique seems simple enough to be used in applications of ResNets, so I would tend towards acceptance of this paper.
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

As mentioned in Section 4, we obtain the stochastic ResNet models in the stochastic Ito ensemble by starting with the weights of a standard ResNet model and training them for 40 epochs with a learning rate of 0.0001 using the Adam optimizer. We will release the code after the paper is accepted. 

* The use of ensembles of several models to provide robustness has been widely used in the machine learning literature before. The authors should review or at least mention other approaches to constructing ensembles and comment on why their method provides an advantage versus existing ones. What is it about adding a Brownian motion term to an SDE that acts to help with improving robustness?

We have compared against the ensemble approach presented in Tianyu Pang, Kun Xu, Chao Du, Ning Chen, and Jun Zhu. Improving adversarial robustness via promoting ensemble diversity. Results in Table 1 show that our approach achieves a robust accuracy of 84.60 while the previous approach has a robustness of 48.4% for the PGD attack on CIFAR-10.

content.title: Clarification on training
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for patience, and we will use the feedback to improve the clarity of the presentation in our paper. 

Our approach to creating ensembles is different from traditional approaches that change the objective to introduce diversity (such as add cosine loss term). Our objective function is still the cross-entropy loss. The different models in the ensemble are created by training the SDE models using different randomly sampled noise injected during the training of the network. While we could explicitly encourage the diversity of models by changing the objective, just utilizing the randomness of injected noise creates a robust ensemble as it forces each model in the ensemble to be robust to different noise. Our goal was to demonstrate the impact of this random ensemble without any introduction of parametric diversity. The injection of noise is controlled by \sigma (diffusion coefficient) as described at the end of Page 3 by sampling the diffusion noise term for each batch. Since the injected noise is through sampling,  the computation of the gradient happens exactly as in a ResNet for each batch except that they are now computed after addition of noise to the samples. In practice, this is achieved by modifying not the objective but instead the ResNet through addition of \sigma controlled random noise at each layer.  This creates an ensemble of SDEs which will converge in their drift behavior but will have different diffusion behavior.

display_title: Scaling noise in Resnets to generate resilience

content.title: Scaling noise in Resnets to generate resilience
content.review:
This paper presents a new class of Resnets, called Ito Ensembles. These Resnets are obtained by adding noise to original Resnets. The key point is that the amplitude of the noise depends on the depth of the layer, and the appropriate scaling with depth is chosen based on arguments from stochastic calculus. Extensive numerical experiments show that the Ito Ensembles vastly outperform state-of-the-art networks in terms of resilience to adversarial attacks, while keeping a very high accuracy on benign inputs.

Altogether, this paper seems like a strong candidate for ICLR. I am however not at all an expert on resilience to advesarial attacks, and therefore not fully qualified to assess the main results (hence my low confidence score). My expertise lies closer to stochastic differential equations, and I mostly comment on this aspect below.

Strengths:
- addresses an important question, the resilience of Resnets
- beyond state-of-art performance on adversarial attacks
- extensive numerical experiments
- possibly principled arguments for noise amplitude (but see below)

Concerns:
- I feel uncomfortable with the insistence on "Ito ensembles" and "Ito calculus". Ito calculus refers to stochastic differential equations obtained by taking a specific continuous limit (in contrast to Stratonovich), and this plays a marginal role here. The Ito Ensemble networks introduced in the paper are in fact simply discrete networks with additive noise, so  calling them "Ito ensembles" is a little misleading.
- the Ito formalism is in fact only used to derive the scaling of the noise term with layer depth. I have however found that part difficult to follow (while it lies close to my expertise). In particular, the specific omega/(1+t) scaling is introduced without motivation, while presumably it should be explainable with a simple scaling argument. I am probably missing something, but it is not completely clear to me how this scaling leads to the final equation, where the depth t is absent. It would be important to make the arguments more transparent, as this is a key part of the paper.
- It would have been interesting to see what happens numerically when the noise follows a different scaling with depth. How much do the resilience/performance results ultimately depend on the specific scaling?


Other feedback:
- the last paragraph before Section 4 is particularly hard to follow: 
	* "interpreting p(x,t) as a function that is constant along trajectories" - not sure what this means, p(x,t) is the density of trajectories
	* "p(x,t) corresponds to the following differential equation ..." - the equation that comes next is simply the equation for the mean trajectory, so again not sure what this is supposed to convey.
- is the argument for noise amplitude specific in any way to Resnets, or does it apply to any deep network?
- Table 5 shows performance as function of w for Imagenet Results. It would have been nice to see it also for Cifar-10
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
* It would have been interesting to see what happens numerically when the noise follows a different scaling with depth. How much do the resilience/performance results ultimately depend on the specific scaling?

We selected the linear scaling to gradually decrease the noise added to internal representations as we go towards the output of the network. Alternative scaling could also be investigated, and we will include these in the final version. 

* the last paragraph before Section 4 is particularly hard to follow:
"interpreting p(x,t) as a function that is constant along trajectories" - not sure what this means, p(x,t) is the density of trajectories
"p(x,t) corresponds to the following differential equation ..." - the equation that comes next is simply the equation for the mean trajectory, so again not sure what this is supposed to convey.

The formulation in Section 3 is the application of transport equations to derive the stochastic PDE model from DNNs. p(x,t) is a function that is constant along the trajectory of the DNN. Intuitively, this is also referred to as level sets. While this formulation has been used previously in deriving PDE representation of neural networks (for e.g. see Equation 7 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.05115.pdf ), our novelty lies in adding Brownian motion to create a stochastic dynamical system and train it to be robust to adversarial attacks.    

* is the argument for noise amplitude specific in any way to Resnets, or does it apply to any deep network?

Translation from neural networks to ODEs is applicable to Resnets and other related architectures such as Spiking-and-Excitation networks. 

* Table 5 shows performance as function of w for Imagenet Results. It would have been nice to see it also for Cifar-10

We have included this in the paper. Figure 4 (right)  in the paper shows the effect of omega (w) for Cifar-10 results.
